newsitem.title: USA: Four-party Korean peace talks open in New York.
newsitem.headline: Four-party Korean peace talks open in New York.

text.p: North Korea on Tuesday opened talks with the United States, South Korea and China aimed at securing peace in the last flashpoint of the Cold War.
Officials from the four states shook hands but gave no hint whether they thought the meeting -- the result of a tortured year-long process -- would be successful.

Their immediate goal was to agree on a specific date, time and agenda for beginning substantive negotiations intended to replace the fraying armistice from the 1950-53 Korean War with a more permanent peace, presumably in the form of a treaty.

"I hope we have a good dialogue today," Song Young Shik, the head of South Korea's delegation said at the start of the preparatory talks that U.S. and South Korean officials expected would last several days.

But as they posed for pictures and handshakes arranged by U.S. delegate Charles Kartman, the four delegation leaders did not respond when asked by a reporter if they believed they could agree on a date to launch the substantive negotiations.
The meeting is being held at Columbia University's School of Public and International Affairs

The United States and South Korea have held a series of meetings since last March to persuade the isolated Stalinist regime in Pyongyang to join the peace process proposed 17 months ago by the U.S. and South Korean presidents.
North Korea finally agreed in June. Tuesday's meeting marks a watershed because it includes China for the first time and is a step closer to launching actual negotiations.

"This is real progress. We have moved from a round table to a square table," Kartman told the delegations in a reference to the presence of China, a North Korea ally and with the United States and the two Koreas a party to the Korean War armistice.

The talks opened one day after North Korea turned over four sets of remains of American servicemen missing from the Korean War and as international relief workers reported that a drought is compounding North Korea's severe food shortages.

Although they acknowledged they could not move about in North Korea freely, the relief officials told journalists the drought was pushing millions of North Koreans to the brink of starvation and that they have not seen such severe malnutrition since recent famines in Ethiopia and Somalia.
To get to Tuesday's "talks about talks," the parties first had to overcome a row caused last year when a North Korean submarine made an incursion into the south.

Beyond that, the main obstacle has been North Korea's demand for food aid to compensate for the famine caused by two years of severe rains and a system that critics say is unable to meet the country's needs.
Washington and Seoul, responding to deprivations authenticated by the U.N. World Food Programme, have provided North Korea with thousands of tons of emergency commodities.
They also made it clear that Pyongyang can expect more long-term assistance as part of the peace talks process.
Nevertheless, U.S. officials would not be surprised if the food aid issue was raised again during this week's talks.
Although doubts remain about Pyongyang's real commitment to reducing tensions on the Korean peninsula, U.S. officials insist that negotiations can still yield positive results.

Presuming the substantive peace talks begin in September, the United States plans to propose new ways to ease tensions between the two Koreas, including such confidence building measures as exchanging military visits and providing advance notification of military manoeuvres.
